title: If a sealed interface has a `non-sealed` implementor, can an unlisted class extend it?
shortTitle: If a sealed interface has a `non-sealed` implementor, can an unlisted class extend it?

s1_definition.profdef: Yes. When a permitted subtype of a sealed interface is declared `non-sealed`, it deliberately reopens the hierarchy at that point, so any class — including one not named anywhere in a `permits` clause — may extend or implement that `non-sealed` type without restriction. The sealing is enforced only at the first level (who may directly implement the sealed interface), but a `non-sealed` branch removes the restriction below it, so unlisted classes can appear beneath the `non-sealed` type while still being, through it, subtypes of the sealed interface.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India seals the list of who may directly be an "Account": only Savings, Current, and a special "Partner" product. For Partner, head office stamps "open policy" (non-sealed), meaning any third-party fintech partner may build their own product on top of Partner without head office approving each one by name. So while nobody new can be a *direct* Account, anyone can build under the open Partner branch, and those partner-built products are still Accounts through Partner. The open stamp on one branch lets unlisted newcomers in beneath it.
s1_definition.oneliner: A `non-sealed` subtype reopens its branch, so any unlisted class may extend it and thereby become an indirect subtype of the sealed interface.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Yes. When a permitted subtype of a sealed interface is declared `non-sealed`, it deliberately reopens the hierarchy at that point, so any class — including one not named anywhere in a `permits` clause — may extend or implement that `non-sealed` type without restriction. The sealing is enforced only at the first level (who may directly implement the sealed interface), but a `non-sealed` branch removes the restriction below it, so unlisted classes can appear beneath the `non-sealed` type while still being, through it, subtypes of the sealed interface.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India seals the list of who may directly be an "Account": only Savings, Current, and a special "Partner" product. For Partner, head office stamps "open policy" (non-sealed), meaning any third-party fintech partner may build their own product on top of Partner without head office approving each one by name. So while nobody new can be a *direct* Account, anyone can build under the open Partner branch, and those partner-built products are still Accounts through Partner. The open stamp on one branch lets unlisted newcomers in beneath it.

**One line to remember:** A `non-sealed` subtype reopens its branch, so any unlisted class may extend it and thereby become an indirect subtype of the sealed interface.

sections.s2_technical:
Sealing restricts **direct** subtypes: the `permits` clause of a sealed interface names exactly which types may directly implement it. Each permitted type must declare `final`, `sealed`, or `non-sealed`. The choice of `non-sealed` is a deliberate statement that **this branch is reopened**: below this type, the normal, unrestricted extension rules apply again, so any class may extend it, and those classes do **not** need to be listed in any `permits` clause.

So the answer to "can an unlisted class extend a `non-sealed` implementor" is **yes**. The unlisted class extends the `non-sealed` type freely, and because the `non-sealed` type is itself a subtype of the sealed interface, the unlisted class is **transitively** a subtype of the sealed interface too. The sealing guarantee that "only the permitted types directly implement the interface" still holds — the unlisted class does not directly implement the sealed interface; it implements the `non-sealed` type, which is permitted.

This has a concrete **consequence for exhaustiveness**. Because a `non-sealed` branch is open, the compiler can **no longer treat the full hierarchy as closed** for the purpose of exhaustive switching down to leaves. When you `switch` over the sealed interface, you can still match the `non-sealed` type itself as one case (covering it and anything beneath it), and that keeps the switch exhaustive at the level of the direct permitted types. But you cannot exhaustively enumerate the unknown classes beneath the `non-sealed` type, because new ones can appear at any time. So `non-sealed` trades some exhaustiveness for extensibility, by design.

The typical **use case** is a library or framework that wants a closed core but one deliberately open extension point. For example, a sealed interface models a closed set of built-in types, and one `non-sealed` member serves as the public base that third parties subclass to plug in their own implementations. This is common for plugin architectures: the vendor controls the closed set, but opens exactly one branch for extension, keeping control while allowing growth.

A senior nuance is that `non-sealed` is the **only** way to let outside, unlisted classes participate in a sealed hierarchy, and it must be used intentionally because it reopens encapsulation at that point. Another nuance is that when switching over a sealed type with a `non-sealed` branch, if you need to handle unknown subtypes you match the `non-sealed` base type as a catch-all for that branch, which keeps type safety while acknowledging the openness. A final nuance is that in a banking domain you use `non-sealed` sparingly and deliberately — for instance a `non-sealed PartnerProduct` branch for third-party integrations — while keeping the regulated core products `final`, so the open branch is isolated and auditable rather than a hole in the whole model.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India seals its `Account` interface so only savings, current, and a partner product may directly be accounts. But the bank wants third-party fintech partners to build their own account products without head office listing each by name. The solution is to make the partner product `non-sealed`, reopening that branch so unlisted partner classes may extend it. This directly answers the question.

Problem 2 — The bank's core products, savings and current, must stay closed and final so no rogue core product appears. Only the partner branch is open. This shows mixing a closed core with one open extension point.

Problem 3 — A handler switching over `Account` must remain type-safe even though partner subtypes are unknown. We match the `non-sealed PartnerProduct` base as one case, which covers it and any unlisted class beneath it, keeping the switch complete at the permitted-type level.

In the mini-project we define a sealed `Account` permitting `SavingsAccount` (final), `CurrentAccount` (final), and `PartnerProduct` (non-sealed). We then add an unlisted `WalletProduct` that extends `PartnerProduct` without being in any permits list, and a handler that switches over `Account` matching the partner base. We log that the unlisted class is a valid `Account`.

The code contains: the sealed `Account`, final core products, a non-sealed partner base, an unlisted partner subclass, a handler, and a demo.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a savings account, a current account, and a `WalletProduct` for partner PayFast that is not listed in any permits clause.

Step 1 — The sealed `Account` permits only savings, current, and partner-product as direct implementors. Savings and current are final, so their branches are closed. The partner product is `non-sealed`, which reopens its branch for unlimited extension.

Step 2 — `WalletProduct` extends `PartnerProduct` without appearing in any permits clause. The compiler accepts this because `PartnerProduct` is `non-sealed`, so unlisted classes may extend it. Transitively, `WalletProduct` is a valid `Account`.

Step 3 — `main` creates one of each and the handler describes them. The switch over `Account` has cases for savings, current, and the partner-product base. Matching the partner base covers the `WalletProduct` instance too, because it is a `PartnerProduct`. The switch remains exhaustive at the permitted-type level even though partner subtypes are open.

Step 4 — The handler prints the partner name for the wallet product by calling the overridden `partnerName`, showing the unlisted class participating fully as an `Account`.

Step 5 — Finally, `instanceof` checks confirm that an unlisted `WalletProduct` is both an `Account` and a `PartnerProduct`, demonstrating the transitive membership granted by the `non-sealed` branch.

```

     │ sealing enforced at DIRECT level only
     ▼
  ┌──────────────┬──────────────┬────────────────────────────┐
  final          final          non-sealed  ← branch REOPENED
  SavingsAccount  CurrentAccount  PartnerProduct
  (closed)        (closed)            │ ANY class may extend, unlisted
                                      ▼
                               WalletProduct  (NOT in any permits)
                                      │ transitively → is-a Account

  describe(a) → switch (exhaustive at permitted level):
     SavingsAccount → "SAVINGS ..."
     CurrentAccount → "CURRENT ..."
     PartnerProduct → covers PartnerProduct AND WalletProduct beneath it
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Yes, if a permitted subtype of a sealed interface is declared non-sealed, then an unlisted class can extend it. Sealing restricts only the direct implementors of the sealed interface through the permits clause, and each permitted type must declare final, sealed, or non-sealed. Choosing non-sealed is a deliberate statement that this branch is reopened, so below that type the normal unrestricted extension rules apply again, and any class may extend it without being listed in any permits clause.

The unlisted class extends the non-sealed type freely, and because the non-sealed type is itself a subtype of the sealed interface, the unlisted class becomes a subtype of the sealed interface transitively. The sealing guarantee still holds, because the unlisted class does not directly implement the sealed interface; it implements the non-sealed type, which is the permitted one. In my banking project I seal Account so only savings, current, and a partner product may directly be accounts, I keep savings and current final, and I make the partner product non-sealed. Then a wallet product from a third-party partner extends the partner product without being listed anywhere, and it is still a valid Account.

The important consequence I mention is about exhaustiveness. Because the non-sealed branch is open, the compiler can no longer treat the whole hierarchy as closed down to the leaves, since new partner subtypes can appear at any time. But when I switch over Account I match the non-sealed partner-product base as one case, which covers it and anything beneath it, so my switch stays exhaustive at the level of the permitted types while still handling unknown partner subclasses. So non-sealed trades some exhaustiveness for extensibility, by design.

The typical use is exactly this: a closed core with one deliberately open extension point, like a plugin architecture where the vendor controls the built-in set and opens one branch for third parties. I use non-sealed sparingly and intentionally, keeping the regulated core products final so the open branch is isolated and auditable rather than a hole in the whole model. That way I let partners extend the system without head office approving each product by name, while the bank still fully controls who may be a direct account.

---

keyPoints: sealed: restrict which classes can extend/implement
permits: explicit list of allowed subclasses
Subclass must be: final, sealed, or non-sealed
Enables exhaustive switch/pattern matching — compiler checks all cases
